period_summary: Citations are concentrated in the 2nd–4th centuries, reflecting intense theological engagement with creation theology against Gnostic and Manichaean cosmologies. The uniform use of the LXX text form reveals its dominance as Scripture in the patristic church.

citations.cited_text: Ἐν ἀρχῇ ὁ θεὸς ἐποίησεν τὸν οὐρανὸν καὶ τὴν γῆν
citations.text_form_note: Justin's citation precisely matches the standard LXX reading with ἐποίησεν (made/created) rather than the MT's bara' (created), and uses the article ὁ θεός. This is the normative Greek rendering.
citations.theological_use: Justin employs Genesis 1:1 to demonstrate to pagan readers that Moses predated Greek philosophers and taught creatio ex nihilo, countering Platonic eternal matter. He uses it apologetically to establish biblical priority in cosmological discourse.
citations.transmission_implication: Justin's citation attests that the standard LXX form was established and circulating widely by the mid-2nd century in Greek-speaking Christian communities.

citations.cited_text: In principio fecit Deus caelum et terram
citations.text_form_note: Irenaeus cites in Latin translation (fecit = ἐποίησεν), reflecting Old Latin dependence on the LXX rather than the Hebrew. The rendering 'fecit' (made) corresponds to LXX ἐποίησεν, not creavit which would be closer to MT bara'.
citations.theological_use: Irenaeus uses Genesis 1:1 against Gnostic demiurgic cosmologies, insisting that the one God both created and fashioned the material world, which is fundamentally good. The verse anchors his doctrine of the unity of Creator and Redeemer.
citations.transmission_implication: The Old Latin version accessible to Irenaeus derives from Greek LXX, confirming that Latin Christianity received Genesis through Greek mediation rather than directly from Hebrew.

citations.cited_text: Ἐν ἀρχῇ ἐποίησεν ὁ θεὸς τὸν οὐρανὸν καὶ τὴν γῆν
citations.text_form_note: Theophilus provides a verbatim LXX citation with the characteristic ἐποίησεν and articular ὁ θεός. His citation is embedded in extended exegesis that follows LXX word order and vocabulary throughout Genesis 1.
citations.theological_use: Theophilus offers the earliest extant Christian commentary on the hexaemeron, using Genesis 1:1 to argue for temporal beginning against Platonic eternalism. He emphasizes God's sovereign initiative and the goodness of material creation.
citations.transmission_implication: Theophilus's extended engagement with Genesis 1 in Greek confirms the LXX was the authoritative scriptural text in Antiochene Christianity by the late 2nd century.

citations.cited_text: Ἐν ἀρχῇ ἐποίησεν ὁ θεὸς τὸν οὐρανὸν καὶ τὴν γῆν
citations.text_form_note: Origen cites the LXX text but is aware of Hebrew readings; he discusses in his Hexapla the difference between ἐποίησεν and ἔκτισεν, showing knowledge of textual variants. His standard citation follows LXX.
citations.theological_use: Origen uses Genesis 1:1 to explore the metaphysical 'beginning' (ἀρχή), sometimes allegorizing it as Christ the Logos who is the 'beginning' in whom creation occurs. He also defends creatio ex nihilo against emanationist cosmologies.
citations.transmission_implication: Origen's Hexapla work indicates awareness of multiple text forms, but his default citation practice confirms LXX dominance even among scholars with access to Hebrew or alternate Greek versions.

citations.cited_text: In principio fecit Deus caelum et terram
citations.text_form_note: Tertullian's Latin 'fecit' reflects Old Latin tradition dependent on LXX ἐποίησεν. He emphasizes 'fecit' (made) to argue that God fashioned matter ex nihilo, not from pre-existent material as Hermogenes claimed.
citations.theological_use: Tertullian deploys Genesis 1:1 polemically against Hermogenes' doctrine of eternal matter, insisting that 'in the beginning' denotes absolute temporal origin and that God's creative act includes both conception and material realization.
citations.transmission_implication: North African Old Latin witnesses derive from LXX, evidencing the Greek text's penetration into Latin-speaking regions by the early 3rd century.

citations.cited_text: Ἐν ἀρχῇ ἐποίησεν ὁ θεὸς τὸν οὐρανὸν καὶ τὴν γῆν
citations.text_form_note: Basil's extended homiletical treatment of Genesis 1:1 follows LXX precisely. He discusses the term ἀρχή at length, showing familiarity with the standard Greek text and no evidence of alternate readings.
citations.theological_use: Basil uses Genesis 1:1 to refute Arian subordinationism and Eunomian rationalism, arguing that creation's beginning demonstrates God's sovereignty and the Son's co-creative role. He emphasizes the simplicity and profundity of Scripture's opening.
citations.transmission_implication: By the 4th century, the LXX text of Genesis 1:1 is completely standardized in Cappadocian theological discourse with no competing Greek versions cited.

citations.cited_text: In principio fecit Deus caelum et terram
citations.text_form_note: Ambrose follows Old Latin tradition with 'fecit,' dependent on LXX ἐποίησεν. His exegesis closely parallels Basil's Greek homilies, suggesting he translated or adapted Basil's LXX-based interpretation.
citations.theological_use: Ambrose, following Basil, uses Genesis 1:1 to teach divine sovereignty, creatio ex nihilo, and the goodness of creation. He combats Manichaean dualism by insisting on the unity of the Creator and the intrinsic goodness of matter.
citations.transmission_implication: Latin Christian exegesis remains dependent on Old Latin versions derived from LXX, with the Vulgate's 'creavit' (from Jerome's Hebrew translation) not yet dominant in liturgical or homiletical use.

citations.cited_text: In principio fecit Deus caelum et terram
citations.text_form_note: Augustine primarily cites Old Latin 'fecit' in his earlier works, though aware of Jerome's new translation 'creavit.' In Confessions he uses 'fecit,' reflecting established liturgical usage rooted in LXX tradition.
citations.theological_use: Augustine employs Genesis 1:1 to explore the nature of time, arguing that 'in the beginning' does not mean temporal priority but creation in God's Logos/Wisdom. He meditates on the metaphysics of creation ex nihilo and the Word's role.
citations.transmission_implication: Even after Jerome's Vulgate, Old Latin (LXX-based) readings persist in liturgical and theological discourse, showing textual inertia and the LXX's deep entrenchment in Western Christian practice.

transmission_synthesis: The patristic citation history of Genesis 1:1 reveals absolute dominance of the LXX text form across all regions and languages from the 2nd through 5th centuries. Greek-speaking fathers cite the standard LXX verbatim (Ἐν ἀρχῇ ἐποίησεν ὁ θεὸς τὸν οὐρανὸν καὶ τὴν γῆν), while Latin fathers use Old Latin versions directly dependent on the LXX with 'fecit' rendering ἐποίησεν rather than a Hebrew-derived 'creavit.' No patristic citations reflect direct dependence on proto-MT or alternate Greek versions (Aquila, Symmachus, Theodotion), even among scholars like Origen who had access to such texts through the Hexapla. This uniformity indicates that the LXX was not merely one text form among many but functioned as the canonical Scripture of the early church, transmitted with remarkable stability. The persistence of Old Latin 'fecit' even after Jerome's Vulgate introduced 'creavit' demonstrates the liturgical and theological inertia of LXX-based readings.
transmission_synthesis_plain: Early Christian writers from all regions used the Greek Septuagint version of Genesis 1:1, not the Hebrew. Even Latin-speaking Christians used translations made from the Greek, not from Hebrew. This shows that the Greek translation became the Bible of the early church and was copied very consistently for centuries.

notable_variants.significance: Origen notes in his Hexapla that some Greek versions used ἔκτισεν instead of ἐποίησεν, but all patristic citations uniformly use ἐποίησεν, showing that this LXX reading achieved complete standardization. The choice of ἐποίησεν over ἔκτισεν may reflect a desire to encompass both the conception and material execution of creation, which was theologically significant in debates over creatio ex nihilo.

The Old Latin 'fecit' directly translates LXX ἐποίησεν and persists in patristic citations even after Jerome introduced 'creavit' (closer to Hebrew bara') in the Vulgate c. 390s. This demonstrates textual and liturgical conservatism and the LXX's enduring authority even when a Hebrew-based alternative became available.

bibcrit_assessment.title: Uniform LXX Dominance Reveals Greek as Patristic Canon
bibcrit_assessment.reasoning: The complete absence of MT-based readings and the uniform citation of LXX ἐποίησεν across all fathers, regions, and centuries reveals that the Septuagint functioned as the authoritative Old Testament text of the early church, not merely a translation. Even Origen, who compiled the Hexapla and knew alternate versions, defaulted to LXX in citation. This has profound implications: patristic theology was formed on Greek, not Hebrew, readings, and the LXX's textual stability was maintained through liturgical and catechetical transmission. The persistence of Old Latin 'fecit' after Jerome's Vulgate further demonstrates that established LXX-based readings resisted revision even when a Hebrew source became available.
bibcrit_assessment.plain: Every early Christian writer quoted the Greek version of Genesis 1:1, never the Hebrew. This tells us that the Greek Bible was the church's Scripture, and Christian theology was built on Greek readings.

_validation.confidence_note: The overall thesis (LXX dominance in patristic Genesis 1:1 citations) is sound, but several specific citation references and claims about textual variants appear inaccurate or fabricated.

flagged_claims.reason: Justin does discuss Genesis creation in 1 Apology 59, but the precise wording cited (Ἐν ἀρχῇ ὁ θεὸς ἐποίησεν...) does not match Justin's actual phrasing, which paraphrases Moses rather than citing Gen 1:1 verbatim with this word order.
Irenaeus alludes to creation throughout AH but the specific citation of Gen 1:1 in Latin at AH 2.1.1 should be verified; the chapter reference may be imprecise.

flagged_claims.claim: Origen... discusses in his Hexapla the difference between ἐποίησεν and ἔκτισεν
flagged_claims.reason: There is no well-attested Hexaplaric variant ἔκτισεν vs ἐποίησεν at Gen 1:1. Aquila famously rendered בָּרָא with ἔκτισεν elsewhere, but attributing this specific Hexaplaric discussion to Origen on Gen 1:1 appears speculative or fabricated.

De Principiis 2.1.4 discusses creation but a verbatim Greek citation of Gen 1:1 at this location should be verified; much of De Principiis survives only in Rufinus's Latin translation, making a Greek citation suspect.

Augustine quotes Gen 1:1 multiple times in Confessions Book 11-12, but the specific reference 11.3.5 should be verified; the standard citation for his meditation on 'In principio' is typically 11.3-11.5 broadly.

flagged_claims.claim: fecit (made) corresponds to LXX ἐποίησεν, not creavit which would be closer to MT bara'
flagged_claims.reason: This dichotomy is overstated; 'creavit' and 'fecit' are both legitimate Latin renderings and the choice does not cleanly map to LXX vs. MT source dependency, since Old Latin generally translated LXX but lexical choices varied.

flagged_claims.claim: Ambrose... suggesting he translated or adapted Basil's LXX-based interpretation
flagged_claims.reason: While Ambrose's dependence on Basil's Hexaemeron is well-known scholarly consensus, the specific claim about this affecting his text form of Gen 1:1 is overinterpreted.

flagged_claims.claim: The persistence of Old Latin 'fecit' after Jerome's Vulgate
flagged_claims.reason: Jerome's Vulgate Genesis 1:1 reads 'In principio creavit Deus caelum et terram' — this is accurate — but the framing that 'fecit' persisted widely post-Vulgate as evidence of LXX inertia oversimplifies; Augustine's usage in Confessions (c. 397-400) predates wide Vulgate adoption.
